When considering the complete DARHT system of systems, four axes in a plane appears to be the realistic limit for the packaging of the accelerator DST, VCS, and GRC systems onto the DARHT firing point. Given this constraint, there are a few options that can be pursued to increase the number of viewing axes at DARHT. Incorporation of a second, and/or third, DST region on A2 can economically enable improved data collection for these 3D scenarios with a modest impact to DARHT operations. It should be noted that the ability to achieve dual, or more, DST regions on A2 is dependent upon successful construction and operation of the MPTL. Alternatively, a Scorpius-type machine could be installed as an independent viewing axis with greater capability, but at a more substantial cost and impact to DARHT operations given the magnitude of construction this would involve. A2 DDST Options Since its original design period, additional viewing axes were conceived of for A2 [Chen, 2000]. At present, less than 20% of the total beam pulse length is transmitted to the DST region of the machine by the kicker. Substantial modifi- cations to the DST portion of A2 could enable a larger fraction of the beam to be used for radiographic interrogation in similar fashion as the present A2. As shown in Figure 13, Axis 2b (A2b) could be coupled to an x-ray converter source and provide penetrating views alongside the original Axis 2a (A2a) view, providing a DDST system. If the DST were modified to provide this second beamline, it could penetrate the DARHT bullnose port plug routed through a second kicker, beam stop, and delay line before heading back to the vessel. No beam optics are shown in Figure 13 because none have been designed at this point. The design and operation of the MPTL previously discussed will provide extremely valuable information on the viability and implementation of a DDST. In addition, only an initial investigation of using the existing kicker beamline hardware, assuming an additional power supply for the horizon- tal kicker electrodes, has been conducted. The investigation indicated a deflection of as much as seven degrees is needed to use the existing septum quadrupole magnet to achieve a horizontal kick that then crosses the axis in the direction of the second port plug.
